nodes.name: Symplectic manifold
nodes.statement: Recall that a symplectic manifold is a smooth even-dimensional manifold $M$, equipped with a closed non-degenerate differential 2-form $\omega$. Non-degeneracy of $\omega$ means that its top wedge power, $\omega^n$, is a volume form.
differentia: equipped with a closed non-degenerate differential 2-form $\omega$

nodes.name: Group of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms Ham(M, omega)
nodes.statement: This is the group of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms, denoted $Ham(M,\omega)$, which plays a central role in symplectic topology and Hamiltonian dynamics.

nodes.name: Hofer's metric
nodes.statement: Recall that Hofer's metric on $Ham(M,\omega)$ is defined as \begin{myequation} d_H(f,g) = \inf_H \int_0^1 \left( \max_M H_t - \min_M H_t \right) dt , \end{myequation} for $f,g \in Ham(M,\omega)$, where the infimum is taken over all smooth $H: S^1 \times M \to \mathbb{R}$ that generate $f^{-1}g$ and where $H_t = H(t,\cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hofer distance $d_H(f,g)$: infimum over Hamiltonians generating $f^{-1}g$ of the integrated oscillation $\max H_t - \min H_t$.

nodes.name: Hofer's metric is a bi-invariant genuine metric
nodes.statement: This is a bi-invariant metric on $Ham(M)$, and the fact that it is a genuine metric, as opposed to a pseudo-metric, is non-trivial (see~\cite{H},\cite{LM}).
conclusions: This is a bi-invariant metric on $Ham(M)$
it is a genuine metric, as opposed to a pseudo-metric

nodes.name: Hofer's norm
nodes.statement: Hofer's norm of a diffeomorphism is its Hofer distance to the identity, and is denoted \[ ||\cdot||_H = d_H(id,\cdot) . \]

nodes.name: Hamiltonian diameter question (Hofer diameter of Ham)
nodes.statement: The question whether for every symplectic manifold $Ham(M)$ has infinite diameter with respect to Hofer's metric is an important open problem in this field; it is conjectured (see discussion in 14.2 of~\cite{MS}) that the answer to this question is positive for every closed symplectic manifold $M$.
nodes.statement_short: Does $Ham(M)$ have infinite Hofer diameter for every closed symplectic manifold? Conjectured yes.

nodes.name: Autonomous diffeomorphisms Aut and k-th powers Powers_k
nodes.statement: A natural set $X$ to ask this question for is $Aut(M,\omega)$, the set of autonomous (i.e. "time-independent") Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms, and another interesting family of sets are the sets $Powers_k = \{\psi^k | \psi \in Ham(M,\omega)\}$ of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms which admit $k^{th}$ roots, for $k \geq 2$ an integer.
also_stated_at: Denote by $Powers_k \subset Ham$ the set of elements admitting a root of degree $k$.

nodes.name: Quantities aut and powers_k
nodes.statement: The quantities queried are the following: \begin{myequation} aut(M,\omega) = \sup_{\phi \in Ham(M, \omega)} d_H(\phi, Aut(M, \omega)) ,\\ powers_k(M,\omega) = \sup_{\phi \in Ham(M, \omega)} d_H(\phi, Powers_k(M,\omega)) .
nodes.statement_short: $aut$ and $powers_k$ are the supremal Hofer distances from a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism to $Aut$ and to $Powers_k$.

nodes.name: aut or powers_k infinite answers the diameter question
nodes.statement: Note that for a symplectic manifold $M$, showing that $aut(M) = \infty$ or that for any $k \geq 2$, $powers_k(M) = \infty$ would answer the Hamiltonian diameter question for $M$.

nodes.name: Polterovich-Shelukhin conjecture aut(M) = infinity
nodes.statement: L. Polterovich and E. Shelukhin conjectured in~\cite{PS14} that $aut(M) = \infty$ for all closed symplectic manifolds, and made a first step in that direction: they show that symplectic surfaces $M$ of genus $\geq 4$ have $powers_k(M) = \infty$ for all $k \geq 2$.
conclusions: $aut(M) = \infty$

nodes.name: Filter on a partially ordered set
nodes.statement: A \textit{filter} on a partially ordered set $(P,\leq)$ is a non-empty proper subset $F \subset P$ that is upward closed and downward directed; i.e. if $x \in F, y \in P, x \leq y$ then $y \in F$, and also $\forall x,y \in F \ \exists z \in F$ such that $z \leq x,y$.

nodes.name: Non-principal ultrafilter
nodes.statement: A \textit{non-principal ultrafilter} on $(P,\leq)$ is a filter $F$ on $(P,\leq)$ such that there is no filter $F^\prime$ on $P$ with $F \subset F^\prime \subset P$, and such that $F$ is not of the form $\{x \in P | y \leq x\}$ for any $y \in P$.
differentia: there is no filter $F^\prime$ on $P$ with $F \subset F^\prime \subset P$
$F$ is not of the form $\{x \in P | y \leq x\}$ for any $y \in P$

nodes.name: Ultralimit
nodes.statement: Given a metric space $(X,d)$, an ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on the power set of the natural numbers $2^{\mathbb{N}}$ (equipped with the inclusion order) and a sequence of points $(x_n)$ in $X$, a point $x \in X$ is the $\mathcal{U}$-\textit{ultralimit} of $(x_n)$, denoted $\lim_\mathcal{U} x_n$, if for any $\epsilon > 0$, $\{n | d(x_n,x) \leq \epsilon\} \in \mathcal{U}$.

nodes.name: Existence of ultralimits of bounded sequences
nodes.statement: The ultralimit does not necessarily exist, but can be shown to exist if $(x_n)$ is bounded.
conclusions: can be shown to exist

nodes.name: Asymptotic cone
nodes.statement: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, fix $\mathcal{U}$ a non-principal ultrafilter on $2^{\mathbb{N}}$, and fix some basepoint $x_0 \in X$. The \textit{asymptotic cone} of $(X,d)$ is a metric space $Cone_\mathcal{U}(X,d)$ whose underlying set is \begin{myequation} \left\{ \left( x_k \right)_{k \in \mathbb{N}} \in X^{\mathbb{N}} \middle| \exists C > 0 \ s.t.\ \forall k: \frac{d(x_k,x_0)}{k} < C \right\} \bigg/ \thicksim , \end{myequation} where $(x_k) \sim (y_k)$ if $\lim_\mathcal{U} \frac{d(x_k,y_k)}{k} = 0$, and whose metric is \begin{myequation} d_\mathcal{U} ([(x_k)], [(y_k)]) = \lim_\mathcal{U} \frac{d(x_k,y_k)}{k} . \end{myequation}
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotic cone: sequences of linear growth modulo sublinear distance, with the ultralimit of $d(x_k,y_k)/k$ as metric.

nodes.name: Asymptotic cone of a bi-invariant metric group is a group
nodes.statement: Assume additionally that $X$ is a group, and that $d$ is a bi-invariant metric. Then $Cone_\mathcal{U}(X,d)$ is also a group, with multiplication \begin{myequation} [(x_k)] \cdot [(y_k)] = [(x_k \cdot y_k)] . \end{myequation}
conclusions: $Cone_\mathcal{U}(X,d)$ is also a group, with multiplication
also_stated_at: Further, according to~\cite{CZ}, any asymptotic cone (in the sense of Gromov, see~\cite{G}) of a group with bi-invariant metric has a natural group structure.

nodes.name: Proof that cone multiplication is well defined
nodes.statement: Since $d$ is bi-invariant, this multiplication is well defined, and $d_\mathcal{U}$ is also bi-invariant.
nodes.statement_short: Bi-invariance of $d$ makes the termwise multiplication well defined and $d_\mathcal{U}$ bi-invariant.

nodes.name: Asymptotic cones as coarse invariants
nodes.statement: Elements of the asymptotic cone represent directions (or rather, velocities) in which one can go to infinity in the base space $X$. For example, bounded metric spaces all have asymptotic cones which are single points, and on the other hand, the asymptotic cone of the hyperbolic plane is a tree with uncountably many branches at each point. The asymptotic cone is an invariant of the coarse structure, or the large-scale properties of a metric space, in the sense that quasi-isometric spaces have the same asymptotic cones (see~\cite{R} for more on coarse structure, asymptotic cones, and quasi-isometry).
nodes.statement_short: Cone elements are directions to infinity; bounded spaces give a point, the hyperbolic plane a tree; quasi-isometric spaces share cones.

nodes.name: Powers_k is infinite for surfaces of genus 2 and 3
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus 2 or 3, equipped with an area form $\sigma$, and $k \geq 2$ an integer. Then $powers_k(\Sigma, \sigma) = \infty$.
assumptions: $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus 2 or 3, equipped with an area form $\sigma$
conclusions: $powers_k(\Sigma, \sigma) = \infty$
nodes.statement_short: On closed surfaces of genus 2 or 3, Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms can be arbitrarily Hofer-far from $k$-th powers.
nodes.label: thm:2

nodes.name: Free group F_2 embeds in the asymptotic cone of Ham for genus 2 and 3
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus 2 or 3, equipped with an area form $\sigma$. Then for any non-principal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $2^{\mathbb{N}}$, there exists a monomorphism $F_2 \hookrightarrow Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(\Sigma), d_H)$.
assumptions: $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus 2 or 3, equipped with an area form $\sigma$
conclusions: there exists a monomorphism $F_2 \hookrightarrow Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(\Sigma), d_H)$
nodes.statement_short: For genus 2 or 3 surfaces, the free group on two generators embeds in every asymptotic cone of $(Ham, d_H)$.
nodes.label: thm:3

nodes.name: aut is infinite for surfaces of genus 2 and 3
nodes.statement: We remark that since $aut(M) \geq powers_k(M)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:2} implies that $aut(\Sigma, \sigma) = \infty$ for any closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ of genus 2 or 3 with an area form $\sigma$.
assumptions: any closed oriented surface $\Sigma$ of genus 2 or 3 with an area form $\sigma$
conclusions: $aut(\Sigma, \sigma) = \infty$

nodes.name: Results survive stabilization by aspherical manifolds
nodes.statement: We remark further that the above results survive stabilization by a closed aspherical symplectic manifold. That is, if $(M,\omega)$ is a symplectic manifold with $\pi_2(M) = 0$ and $\Sigma$ is as above, then the results also hold for the symplectic manifold $(\Sigma \times M, \sigma \oplus \omega)$.
conclusions: the results also hold for the symplectic manifold $(\Sigma \times M, \sigma \oplus \omega)$

nodes.name: Proof of stabilization (as in PS14, [10])
nodes.statement: This is shown in the same way as in~\cite{PS14},\cite{10}.
nodes.statement_short: By the same argument as in the cited works.

nodes.name: Incompressible embedding into genus 2
nodes.statement: It is likely that there also exists an embedding $i_2$ into $\Sigma_2$ with an injective $\tau_{i_2}$. However, this isn't proven in this paper.
nodes.section: 1.4 Outline of the proofs for genera 2,3
conclusions: there also exists an embedding $i_2$ into $\Sigma_2$ with an injective $\tau_{i_2}$

nodes.name: Homomorphism i_* : F_3 -> pi_1(Sigma_2)
nodes.statement: One may choose $i$ such that the induced homomorphism $i_*: F_3 = \langle a,b,c \rangle \to \langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4] \rangle$ is the following: \begin{myequation} a \mapsto g_1 g_3 ,\\ b \mapsto g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3 ,\\ c \mapsto g_3 . \end{myequation}
nodes.section: 1.4 Outline of the proofs for genera 2,3

nodes.name: Conjugacy-injectivity lemma for i_* on special words
nodes.statement: Let $p \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}$. For all $1 \leq j \leq p$, let $k_j,l_j \in \mathbb{Z}, u_j,v_j \in \{0,1\}, 0 \neq m_j,n_j \in \mathbb{Z}$. Consider the homomorphism $i_*: F_3 \to \pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ given above. Let $\delta = \Pi_j a^{k_j}c^{-u_j}b^{l_j}c^{v_j} \in F_3$ and $\beta = \Pi_j a^{m_j}b^{n_j} \in F_3$. If $i_* \delta, i_* \beta$ are conjugates (in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$), then so are $\delta, \beta$ (in $F_3$).
nodes.section: 1.4 Outline of the proofs for genera 2,3
conclusions: so are $\delta, \beta$ (in $F_3$)
nodes.statement_short: If the images under $i_*$ of words of the forms $\delta$ and $\beta$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$, then $\delta,\beta$ are conjugate in $F_3$.
nodes.label: lemma:2

nodes.name: Free product with amalgamation
nodes.statement: Let $G,H$ be finitely presentable groups, $A < G, B < H$ be isomorphic subgroups, and $\psi: A \xrightarrow{\sim} B$ an isomorphism. The \textit{free product of $G,H$ with respect to $\psi$} (or free product of $G,H$ with amalgamation), denoted $\langle G * H, A = B, \psi \rangle$, is defined as follows. If $G = \langle S_1 | R_1 \rangle, H = \langle S_2 | R_2 \rangle$ are finite presentations with $S_1 \cap S_2 = \emptyset$, then the free product with amalgamation is defined to be \[ \langle G * H, A = B, \psi \rangle = \langle S_1 \cup S_2 | R_1, R_2, \{a \psi(a)^{-1} | a \in A\} \rangle . \]
nodes.origin_citation: Lyndon & Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, ch. IV
nodes.definiendum: free product of $G,H$ with respect to $\psi$
nodes.statement_short: Amalgamated free product: union of presentations of $G,H$ plus relations identifying $a$ with $\psi(a)$.

nodes.name: Factors of an amalgamated free product
nodes.statement: The groups $G$ and $H$ are called the \textit{factors} of $\langle G * H, A = B, \psi \rangle$.
nodes.origin_citation: Lyndon & Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, ch. IV

nodes.name: van Kampen theorem
nodes.statement: Free products with amalgamation occur naturally in topology: let $X$ is a topological space with open cover $\{Y,Z\}$ such that $Y \cap Z$ is connected, and denote $G = \pi_1(Y), H = \pi_1(Z)$; $A = \pi_1(Y \cap Z)$, considered as a subgroup of $G$; and $B = \pi_1(Y \cap Z)$, considered as a subgroup of $H$. Denote also by $\psi: A \xrightarrow{\sim} B$ the natural isomorphism. Then by the van Kampen theorem: \[ \pi_1(X) = \langle G * H, A = B, \psi \rangle . \]
assumptions: $X$ is a topological space with open cover $\{Y,Z\}$ such that $Y \cap Z$ is connected
conclusions: \pi_1(X) = \langle G * H, A = B, \psi \rangle .
nodes.statement_short: For an open cover with connected intersection, $\pi_1(X)$ is the free product of the pieces' groups amalgamated over the intersection's group.

nodes.name: Reduced and cyclically reduced sequences and elements
nodes.statement: A sequence $c_1,...,c_n$ (with $n \geq 0$) of elements of $\langle G*H, A=B, \psi \rangle$ is called reduced if: \begin{enumerate} \item Each $c_i$ is in one of the factors $G$ or $H$. \item Successive $c_i,c_{i+1}$ come from different factors. \item If $n > 1$, no $c_i$ is in $A$ or $B$. \item If $n = 1$, $c_1 \neq 1$. \end{enumerate} A sequence $c_1,...,c_n$ of elements of $\langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ is called cyclically reduced if all its cyclic permutations (i.e. $c_2,...,c_n,c_1$, etc.) are reduced. An element $u \in \langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ is called cyclically reduced if there exists a cyclically reduced sequence $c_1,...,c_n$ such that $u = c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_n$ (in this case the sequence $(c_i)_{i=1}^n$ is said to represent $u$).
nodes.origin_citation: Lyndon & Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, ch. IV
nodes.statement_short: Reduced sequences alternate factors and avoid the amalgamated subgroup; cyclically reduced means all cyclic permutations are reduced.

nodes.name: Every element is conjugate to a cyclically reduced element
nodes.statement: We remark that every element of $\langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ is conjugate to a (not necessarily unique) cyclically reduced element.
nodes.origin_citation: Lyndon & Schupp, Combinatorial Group Theory, ch. IV
conclusions: every element of $\langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ is conjugate to a (not necessarily unique) cyclically reduced element

nodes.name: Conjugacy Theorem for Free Products with Amalgamation
nodes.statement: Let $P = \langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ be a free product with amalgamation. Let $u \in P$ be a cyclically reduced element, and let $c_1, ..., c_n$ be any cyclically reduced sequence with $u = c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_n$ where $n \geq 2$. Then every cyclically reduced conjugate of $u$ can be obtained by cyclically permuting $c_1 \cdot \cdot \cdot c_n$ and then conjugating by an element of the amalgamated part~$A$: if $v \in P$ is cyclically reduced and conjugate to $u$, then $\exists 0 \leq k < n$ and $\exists a \in A$ such that $v = a \cdot c_k \cdot ... \cdot c_n \cdot c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_{k-1} a^{-1}$.
assumptions: $P = \langle G * H, A = B, \phi \rangle$ be a free product with amalgamation
$u \in P$ be a cyclically reduced element
$c_1, ..., c_n$ be any cyclically reduced sequence with $u = c_1 \cdot ... \cdot c_n$ where $n \geq 2$
conclusions: every cyclically reduced conjugate of $u$ can be obtained by cyclically permuting $c_1 \cdot \cdot \cdot c_n$ and then conjugating by an element of the amalgamated part~$A$
nodes.statement_short: Cyclically reduced conjugates of $u$ are cyclic permutations of its reduced form, conjugated by an element of the amalgamated subgroup.

nodes.name: Conjugacy relation notation
nodes.statement: Denote the conjugacy relation in a group by $\sim$.

nodes.name: Conjugacy class notation [x]_G
nodes.statement: For any group $G$, denote the conjugacy class of an element $x \in G$ by $[x]_G$.

nodes.name: Length function len on an amalgamated free product
nodes.statement: The Conjugacy Theorem implies one can define a length on elements of $P = \langle G*H , A=B, \phi \rangle$ by \begin{myequation} len: P \to \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} ,\\ u \mapsto n , \end{myequation} where $n$ is the length of a cyclically reduced sequence $c_1,...,c_n$ such that $u \sim \Pi_j c_j$.
nodes.statement_short: $len(u)$ is the length of a cyclically reduced sequence whose product is conjugate to $u$.

nodes.name: len is well defined and conjugation-invariant
nodes.statement: This is well defined by the Conjugacy Theorem, and is obviously conjugation-invariant.
conclusions: This is well defined
is obviously conjugation-invariant

nodes.name: len characterizes trivial and factor elements
nodes.statement: Note that $len(u) = 0 \iff u = 1$ and $len(u) = 1$ if and only if $u$ is conjugate to an element of $G \cup H \subset P$.
conclusions: $len(u) = 0 \iff u = 1$
$len(u) = 1$ if and only if $u$ is conjugate to an element of $G \cup H \subset P$

nodes.name: Groups H_1, H_2, A, B and isomorphism phi
nodes.statement: Let us denote the following groups: \begin{myequation} H_1 = \langle g_1, g_2 \rangle \simeq F_2 , \ H_2 = \langle g_3, g_4 \rangle \simeq F_2 ,\\ A = \langle [g_1,g_2] \rangle < H_1 , \ B = \langle [g_3,g_4] \rangle < H_2 , \end{myequation} and denote by $\phi: A \to B$ the isomorphism $[g_1,g_2] \mapsto [g_3,g_4]^{-1}$.

nodes.name: F_3 and pi_1(Sigma_2) as amalgamated product
nodes.statement: Let $F_3 = \langle a,b,c \rangle$ be the free group with three generators, and let $\pi_1(\Sigma_2) = \langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4 \rangle = \langle H_1 * H_2, A = B, \phi \rangle$ be the first homotopy group of a closed oriented surface of genus 2.

nodes.name: Homomorphism varphi : F_3 -> pi_1(Sigma_2)
nodes.statement: Consider the homomorphism $\varphi: F_3 \to \pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ defined by \begin{myequation} a \mapsto g_1 ,\\ b \mapsto g_2 g_1 g_2^{-1} ,\\ c \mapsto g_3 . \end{myequation}

Let $r,s \in F_3$, and assume that $\varphi(r) \sim \varphi(s)$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ and $r

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2.2
nodes.statement:
Note that $\varphi(a)$ and $\varphi(b)$ are both elements in the same factor $H_1$, and $\varphi(c) \in H_2$. Partition $r$ and $s$ into sequences according to the partition $\{a,b,c\} = \{a,b\} \cup \{c\}$, i.e. concatenate consecutive symbols from $\langle a,b angle$, then perform the following steps, until no steps can be performed:  egin{itemize} \item Concatenate elements of the sequence of the form $(ab^{-1})^j$ (for some $j \in \mathbb{Z}$) to the previous and next elements in the sequence; do this for all occurrences of $(ab^{-1})^j$. I.e, if the sequence is $g_1, h_1, ab^{-1}, h_2, (ab^{-1})^{-2}, h_3$ (with all $g_i \in \langle a,b angle, h_i \in \langle c angle$), the resulting sequence after this step will be $g_1, h_1 ab^{-1} h_2 (ab^{-1})^{-2} h_3$. \item If the first and last elements of the sequence are from the same factor (in $\{a,b\},\{c\}$), concatenate them cyclically: i.e, if the sequence is $ab, c, b$, the resulting sequence after this step will be $bab, c$. \end{itemize} Doing this results in sequences $(r_i)_{i=1}^n,(s_i)_{i=1}^m$ such that $r \sim \Pi_i r_i, s \sim \Pi_i s_i$ (in $F_3$) and the sequences $(\varphi(r_i)), (\varphi(s_i))$ are cyclically reduced in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ (since the only way to generate an element of $A$ or $B$ from images of $a,b,c$ is $\varphi(ab^{-1})^j = [g_1,g_2]^j \in A$; this can be seen from the definition of $\varphi$). For example, if $r$ were the element $abcba^{-1}cac^{-1}b$, we first partition according to $\{a,b\},\{c\}$ to get $ab, c, ba^{-1}, c, a, c^{-1}, b$, then concatenate powers of $ab^{-1}$ to get $ab, cba^{-1}c, a, c^{-1}, b$, and finally concatenate the first and last elements to get the sequence $(r_i) = bab, cba^{-1}c, a, c^{-1}$. Note that the resulting sequence is not uniquely defined, but any sequence which is the result of these steps will do for our purposes. \ Now $(\varphi(r_i)), (\varphi(s_i))$ are cyclically reduced sequences of $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$, and $\Pi_{i=1}^m \varphi(s_i) \sim \varphi(s) \sim \varphi(r) \sim \Pi_{i=1}^n \varphi(r_i)$. Assume $n \geq 2$, we will reach a contradiction. By the Conjugacy Theorem for Free Products with Amalgamation, $\exists \alpha \in A, 0 \leq k < n$ such that  egin{equation} \Pi_i \varphi(s_i) = \alpha \cdot \varphi(r_k) \varphi(r_{k+1}) ... \varphi(r_n) \varphi(r_1) ... \varphi(r_{k-2}) \varphi(r_{k-1}) \cdot \alpha^{-1} . \end{equation} Since $A \subset \mathrm{Im} \varphi$, $\alpha = \varphi(\sigma)$ for some $\sigma \in F_3$. Therefore, pulling back Equation~ef{eq:1} through $\varphi$, we get the following equation in $F_3$:  egin{myequation} \Pi_i s_i = \sigma \cdot r_k r_{k+1} ... r_{k-2} r_{k-1} \sigma^{-1} . \end{myequation} Note that this can be done since $\varphi$ is a monomorphism. Now, it can be seen that $s \sim \Pi_i s_i = \sigma r_k r_{k+1} ... r_{k-2} r_{k-1} \sigma^{-1} \sim r$ in $F_3$, contradicting our assumption. Therefore, $n \leq 1$. By symmetry of the above argument with respect to $r$ and $s$, $m \leq 1$ as well. If $m = 0$ or $n = 0$, we get that either $r=1$ or $s=1$, which is a contradiction to the assumptions, so $m = n = 1$. \ Since $n = m = 1$, our sequences from above are $(r_i) = (r), (s_i) = (s)$, so by construction $\varphi(r), \varphi(s)$ are in one of the factors $H_1,H_2$. We shall consider the case $\varphi(r),\varphi(s) \in H_1$ and conclude that $\exists j \in \mathbb{Z} : \varphi(r),\varphi(s) \sim g_1^j$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$. The other case, where $\varphi(r),\varphi(s) \in H_2$ and we conclude that $\exists j \in \mathbb{Z} : \varphi(r),\varphi(s) \sim g_3^j$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_2)$), is analogous. Since $\varphi(r),\varphi(s) \in H_1$, note that $r,s \in \langle a,b angle$. Recall, it was assumed that $r 
ot\sim s$ and $\varphi(r) \sim \varphi(s)$, and want to show that $\exists j \in \mathbb{Z}: \varphi(r), \varphi(s) \sim g_1^j$. Denote $G = \langle a,b angle$, and $\psi = \varphi estriction_G : G 	o H_1$. Note that the conjugacy classes of $G$ are:  egin{enumerate} \item $[1]_G$; \item $[\Pi_i a^{k_i}b^{l_i}]_G$ for some $0 
eq k_i,l_i \in \mathbb{Z}$; \item $[a^k]_G$ for some $0 
eq k \in \mathbb{Z}$; \item $[b^l]_G$ for some $0 
eq l \in \mathbb{Z}$, \end{enumerate} where some of the conjugacy classes listed in case 2 above are not distinct (i.e. $[aba^2b^2]_G = [a^2b^2ab]_G$); this will not matter to our argument. Define $	ilde{\psi}$, a function from the set of conjugacy classes of $G$ to the set of conjugacy classes of $H_1$, by  egin{myequation} 	ilde{\psi}([x]_G) = [\psi(x)]_{H_1} . \end{myequation} Our assumptions can be rewritten as $[r]_G 
eq [s]_G, 	ilde{\psi}([r]_G) = 	ilde{\psi}([s]_G)$, and we want to show $	ilde{\psi}([r]_G) = [g_1^j]_{H_1}$ for some $0 
eq j \in \mathbb{Z}$. Calculate $	ilde{\psi}$ for all the conjugacy classes of $G$ as listed above:  egin{enumerate} \item $	ilde{\psi}([1]_G) = [1]_{H_1}$; \item $	ilde{\psi}([\Pi_i a^{k_i}b^{l_i}]_G) = [\Pi_i g_1^{k_i} g_2 g_1^{l_i} g_2^{-1}]_{H_1}$ ($ orall i: 0 
eq k_i,l_i \in \mathbb{Z}$); \item $	ilde{\psi}([a^k]_G) = [g_1^k]_{H_1}$ ($0 
eq k \in \mathbb{Z}$); \item $	ilde{\psi}([b^l]_G) = [g_2 g_1^l g_2^{-1}]_{H_1} = [g_1^l]_{H_1}$ ($0 
eq l \in \mathbb{Z}$). \end{enumerate} Therefore:  egin{enumerate} \item If $	ilde{\psi}([r]_G) = 	ilde{\psi}([s]_G) = [1]_{H_1}$, then $\psi(r) = \psi(s) = 1$ and then $r = s = 1$ (since $\psi$ is a monomorphism), in contradiction. \item If $	ilde{\psi}([r]_G) = 	ilde{\psi}([s]_G) = [\Pi_i g_1^{k_i} g_2 g_1^{l_i} g_2^{-1}]_{H_1}$, then $[r]_G = [s]_G = [\Pi_i a^{k_i}b^{l_i}]_G$, in contradiction. \end{enumerate} The only cases which are left are $	ilde{\psi}([r]_G) = 	ilde{\psi}([s]_G) = [g_1^j]$ for some $0

nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $r,s$ as sequences whose images are cyclically reduced; the Conjugacy Theorem forces length 1, then classify conjugacy classes of $\langle a,b\rangle$. Key step: pulling the conjugacy back through the monomorphism $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Conjugacy Theorem applied to images of r, s
nodes.statement: \Pi_i \varphi(s_i) = \alpha \cdot \varphi(r_k) \varphi(r_{k+1}) ... \varphi(r_n) \varphi(r_1) ... \varphi(r_{k-2}) \varphi(r_{k-1}) \cdot \alpha^{-1} .
nodes.label: eq:1

nodes.name: Generalization of Claim 2.2 to genus n
nodes.statement: In exactly the same way, one can prove the following: Let $n \geq 2$, and define \begin{myequation} \varphi: F_{2n-1} = \langle a_1,...,a_{2n-1} \rangle \to \pi_1(\Sigma_n) = \langle g_1,...,g_{2n} | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4]...[g_{2n-1},g_{2n}] \rangle ,\\ a_{2i-1} \mapsto g_{2i-1} \ (\forall 1 \leq i \leq n) ,\\ a_{2i} \mapsto g_{2i} g_{2i-1} g_{2i}^{-1} \ (\forall 1 \leq i < n) . \end{myequation} Let $r,s \in F_{2n-1}$, and assume that $\varphi(r) \sim \varphi(s)$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_n)$ and $r \not\sim s$ in $F_{2n-1}$. Then $\exists 1 \leq i \leq n, 0 \neq j \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\varphi(r),\varphi(s) \sim g_{2i-1}^j$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_n)$. \\
conclusions: $\exists 1 \leq i \leq n, 0 \neq j \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $\varphi(r),\varphi(s) \sim g_{2i-1}^j$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma_n)$
nodes.statement_short: For the analogous map $F_{2n-1}\to\pi_1(\Sigma_n)$, merged conjugacy classes are only those of powers of $g_{2i-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.3
nodes.statement:
Define  egin{myequation} A : F_3 	o F_3 ,\ a \mapsto ac ,\ b \mapsto b^{-1}c ,\ c \mapsto c . \end{myequation} This is an automorphism of $F_3$. Note that $i_* = \varphi \circ A$ (with $\varphi$ as defined above). We want to use Claim~ef{cl:1} with $r = A( eta), s = A(\delta)$:  egin{myequation} A( eta) = (ac)^{m_1} (b^{-1}c)^{n_1} ... (ac)^{m_p} (b^{-1}c)^{n_p} ,\ A(\delta) = (ac)^{k_1} c^{-u_1} (b^{-1}c)^{l_1} c^{v_1} ... (ac)^{k_p} c^{-u_p} (b^{-1}c)^{l_p} c^{v_p} . \end{myequation} Assume by contradiction that $\delta 
ot\sim  eta$ in $F_3$. Then $A( eta) 
ot\sim A(\delta)$ in $F_3$, since $A$ is an automorphism of $F_3$, and then by Claim~ef{cl:1}, $\exists 0 
eq j \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that one of the following holds:  egin{itemize} \item $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [c^j]_{F_3}$; \item $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [(ab^{-1}c)^j]_{F_3}$; \item $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [b^j]_{F_3}$; \item $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [a^j]_{F_3}$. \end{itemize} To see that, for example, $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [c^j]_{F_3}$ leads to a contradiction, consider the projection  egin{myequation} p_{a,b} : \langle a,b,c angle 	o \langle a,b angle ,\ a \mapsto a, b \mapsto b, c \mapsto 1 . \end{myequation} If $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [c^j]_{F_3}$, then $[(a)^{m_1} (b^{-1})^{n_1} ... (a)^{m_p} (b^{-1})^{n_p}]_{\langle a,b angle} = [p_{a,b}(A( eta))]_{\langle a,b angle} = [p_{a,b}(c^j)]_{\langle a,b angle} = [1]_{\langle a,b angle}$. This implies that at least one of the $m_i,n_i$ is $0$, else no cancellation can occur in $(a)^{m_1} (b^{-1})^{n_1} ... (a)^{m_p} (b^{-1})^{n_p}$. This is a contradiction to the assumption $ orall i: 0 
eq m_i,n_i$. The other three cases are dealt with similarly: the case $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [(ab^{-1}c)^j]_{F_3}$ using the projection  egin{myequation} p_{ab^{-1}c,c} : \langle a,b,c angle 	o \langle a,b angle ,\ ab^{-1}c \mapsto a, c \mapsto b, a \mapsto 1 . \end{myequation} (note this is well defined since $\{ab^{-1}c, a, c\}$ is a basis of $F_3$), and the cases $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [b^j]_{F_3}$, $[A( eta)]_{F_3} = [a^j]_{F_3}$ using $p_{a,b}$ defined above. nodes.statement_short: Write $i_* = \varphi\circ A$ for an automorphism $A$, apply Claim 2.2, and rule out each exceptional class by projecting to a free factor.

nodes.name: Length of products of images of a and b exceeds 1
nodes.statement: Let $r \in \mathbb{N}, k_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for $i \in \{1,...,2r\}$ with $|k_i| \geq 2$ for all $i$, and consider $\pi_1(\Sigma_2) = \langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4] \rangle$. Then \[ len \left( \Pi_{i=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2i-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2i}} \right) > 1 . \]
nodes.statement_short: Words in the images of $a,b$ with all exponents of size at least 2 have amalgamated length greater than 1.
nodes.label: cl:length

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2.3
nodes.statement: Denote $\epsilon_i = sign(k_i) = \frac{k_i}{|k_i|}$. Consider \begin{myequation} p_{13}: \pi_1(\Sigma_2) \to F_2 = \langle h_1, h_3 \rangle ,\\ g_1 \mapsto h_1 ,\\ g_3 \mapsto h_3 ,\\ g_2, g_4 \mapsto 1 . \end{myequation} Denote $w = \Pi_{i=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2i-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3)^{k_{2i}}$. Assume by contradiction $len(w) \leq 1$. Note that $p_{13}$ preserves factors, i.e. $p_{13}(H_1) = \langle h_1 \rangle, p_{13}(H_2) = \langle h_3 \rangle$. If $len(w) = 0$, then $w = 1$, so $p_{13}(w) = 1$, and then $len(p_{13}(w)) = 0$. Else, $len(w) = 1$, so $w \sim c_1$ with $c_1 \in H_1 < \pi_1(\Sigma_2)$ or $c_1 \in H_2 < \pi_1(\Sigma_2)$. WLOG assume $c_1 \in H_1$. Then $p_{13}(w) \sim p_{13}(c_1) \in p_{13}(H_1) = \langle h_1 \rangle$, and then $len(p_{13}(w)) = 1$. One reaches the same conclusion in both cases: $len(p_{13}(w)) \leq 1$ (note that this is $len$ in $F_2$, which is a free product of $\mathbb{Z} = \langle h_1 \rangle$ with $\mathbb{Z} = \langle h_3 \rangle$ and so is trivially a free product with amalgamation). As a remark, this procedure can be applied for any factor-preserving homomorphism $\psi$ to get $len(g) = len(\psi(g))$. Consider $p_{13}(w)$: \[ p_{13}(w) = \Pi_{i=1}^r (h_1 h_3)^{k_{2i-1}} (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{k_{2i}} . \] This element is made of blocks: $(h_1 h_3)^{k_j}$ or $(h_1^{-1} h_3)^{k_j}$. Each of these blocks is reduced, so the only cancellations in the form of $p_{13}(w)$ given above can happen between two blocks. These are the options for cancellations between two blocks: \begin{itemize} \item If the first block is $(h_1 h_3)^{k_i}$ and the second is $(h_1^{-1} h_3)^{k_{i+1}}$, one of the following holds: \begin{myequation} \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1 h_3)^{|k_i|} (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations} ; \\ \epsilon_i = -\epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1 h_3)^{|k_i|} (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow (h_1 h_3)^{|k_i|-1} h_1 h_1 (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|+1} \ (*) ; \\ - \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1 h_3)^{-|k_i|} (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations} ; \\ \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = -1: (h_1 h_3)^{-|k_i|} (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations}. \end{myequation} Every cancellation of type $(*)$ results in a reduced block starting and ending with $h_1$. Before it comes either $h_3$ or $h_1$ (since $(h_1^{-1} h_3)^{k_{i-1}}$ ends with one of these symbols), and after it comes either $h_1$ or $h_3^{-1}$ (for similar reasons). Thus after a cancellation of this type, none of the two ends of the resulting reduced block can be cancelled any further. \item If the first block is $(h_1^{-1} h_3)^{k_i}$ and the second is $(h_1 h_3)^{k_{i+1}}$, one of the following holds: \begin{myequation} \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{|k_i|} (h_1 h_3)^{|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations} ; \\ \epsilon_i = -\epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{|k_i|} (h_1 h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{|k_i|-1} h_1^{-1} h_1^{-1} (h_1 h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|+1} \ (**) ; \\ - \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = 1: (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{-|k_i|} (h_1 h_3)^{|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations} ; \\ \epsilon_i = \epsilon_{i+1} = -1: (h_1^{-1} h_3)^{-|k_i|} (h_1 h_3)^{-|k_{i+1}|} \rightsquigarrow \text{no cancellations}. \end{myequation} Every cancellation of type $(**)$ results in a reduced block starting and ending with $h_1^{-1}$. Before it comes either $h_3$ or $h_1^{-1}$ and after it comes either $h_1^{-1}$ or $h_3^{-1}$ (for reasons similar to above). Thus after a cancellation of this type, none of the two ends of the resulting reduced block can be cancelled any further. \end{itemize} Therefore, after at most $2r-1$ cancellations one reaches a reduced word. If it is not cyclically reduced, conjugate by the first block and perform one more reduction to get a cyclically reduced word $v$, conjugate to $p_{13}(w)$. Since every reduced block $(*)$ or $(**)$ above has length at least 2, and these are inserted without cancellations to our word $v$, we have $len(p_{13}(w)) = len(v) \geq 2 > 1$. This is a contradiction, so the initial assumption $len(w) \leq 1$ is false.
nodes.statement_short: Project by the factor-preserving map $p_{13}$ to $F_2$ and show the image word stays of length at least 2 after all possible cancellations.

nodes.name: Induced maps tau_f and eta_{M,x} on free loop classes
nodes.statement: A continuous map between two manifolds $f: M \to N$ induces a map $\tau_f: \pi_0(\mathscr{L}M) \to \pi_0(\mathscr{L}N)$ by $\tau_f([\gamma]) = [f \circ \gamma]$, for $\gamma: S^1 \to M$. \\ For any manifold $M$ and point $x \in M$, define the map \begin{myequation} \eta_{M,x} : \pi_1(M,x) \to \pi_0(\mathscr{L}M) , \\ [\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_1(M,x)} \mapsto [\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}M)}. \end{myequation} where $\tilde{\gamma}: S^1 \to M$ is a loop.
nodes.statement_short: $\tau_f$ pushes free homotopy classes of loops forward along $f$; $\eta_{M,x}$ forgets the basepoint of a based loop class.

nodes.name: Naturality square for eta commutes
nodes.statement: Note that the following diagram commutes for any continuous map $f: M \to N$: \begin{center}\begin{tikzcd} \pi_1(M,x) \arrow[r, "f_*"] \arrow[d, "\eta_{M,x}"] & \pi_1(N,f(x)) \arrow[d, "\eta_{N,f(x)}"] \\ \pi_0(\mathscr{L}M) \arrow[r, "\tau_f"] & \pi_0(\mathscr{L}N) \end{tikzcd}\end{center}
conclusions: the following diagram commutes for any continuous map $f: M \to N$

nodes.name: eta identifies exactly conjugate elements
nodes.statement: Note additionally that for $\alpha, \beta \in \pi_1(M,x)$, $\eta_{M,x}(\alpha) = \eta_{M,x}(\beta)$ if and only if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(M,x)$.
conclusions: $\eta_{M,x}(\alpha) = \eta_{M,x}(\beta)$ if and only if $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(M,x)$

nodes.name: Balanced word
nodes.statement: A word $w \in F_2 = \langle V,H \rangle$ is called \textit{balanced} if it is of the form $w = V^{N_1} H^{M_1} ... V^{N_r} H^{M_r}$ for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $N_j,M_j \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$.
differentia: of the form $w = V^{N_1} H^{M_1} ... V^{N_r} H^{M_r}$ for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$, $N_j,M_j \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$

nodes.name: Balanced words are cyclically reduced
nodes.statement: Note that any balanced word is cyclically reduced.
conclusions: any balanced word is cyclically reduced

nodes.name: Non-degenerate fixed point
nodes.statement: Let $\varphi: M \to M$ be a diffeomorphism. A fixed point $x$ of $\varphi$ is called non-degenerate if $d\varphi_x$ does not have 1 as an eigenvalue.
differentia: $d\varphi_x$ does not have 1 as an eigenvalue

nodes.name: Condition for pushing forward along an embedding
nodes.statement: Let $X,Y$ be compact topological spaces, and $i: X \hookrightarrow Y$ a continuous embedding. Let $f: X \to \mathbb{R}$ be a continuous map on $X$, and assume the following condition holds: \begin{equation} \text{For any path-component $C$ of $Y \setminus i(X)$, $f \restriction_{i^{-1}(\partial C)}$ is constant.} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Condition: f constant on preimages of boundaries of complement components
nodes.statement: \text{For any path-component $C$ of $Y \setminus i(X)$, $f \restriction_{i^{-1}(\partial C)}$ is constant.}
nodes.label: eq:condition

nodes.name: Path components C_y and domain D_i
nodes.statement: Let $C_y$ be the path-component of $Y$ that contains $y \in Y$, and denote $D_i = \bigcup_{y \in \mathrm{Im}(i)} C_y \subseteq Y$.

nodes.name: Retracting paths gamma_{i,y}
nodes.statement: For all $y \in D_i$, denote by $\gamma_{i,y}: [0,1] \to C_y$ a continuous path with $\gamma_{i,y}(0) = y$, $\gamma_{i,y}(1) \in \mathrm{Im}(i)$, and such that if $\gamma_{i,y}(t) \in \mathrm{Im}(i)$ for some $t \in [0,1]$, then $\gamma_{i,y} \restriction_{[t,1]}$ is constant.

nodes.name: Endpoint map b_i
nodes.statement: Denote the following, not necessarily continuous, map: \begin{myequation} b_i: D_i \to \mathrm{Im}(i) ,\\ y \mapsto \gamma_{i,y}(1) . \end{myequation}

nodes.name: Pushforward of a function through an embedding
nodes.statement: Define the following map, the \textit{pushforward} of $f$ through $i$: \begin{myequation} i_* f: D_i \to \mathbb{R} ,\\ y \mapsto f \circ i^{-1} \circ b_i(y) . \end{myequation}
nodes.statement_short: $i_* f(y) = f(i^{-1}(b_i(y)))$: extend $f$ from the image of $i$ along retracting paths.

nodes.name: Pushforward is continuous and well defined
nodes.statement: By Condition~\ref{eq:condition}, this is a continuous map $D_i \to \mathbb{R}$ which is constant on $Y \setminus i(X)$, and doesn't depend on the choice of the $\gamma_{i,y}$s.
conclusions: this is a continuous map $D_i \to \mathbb{R}$ which is constant on $Y \setminus i(X)$
doesn't depend on the choice of the $\gamma_{i,y}$s

nodes.name: Pushforward of a smooth function is smooth
nodes.statement: Note also that if $f$ is smooth and constant in a neighborhood of $i^{-1}(\partial \ i(X))$ then $i_* f$ is also smooth.
assumptions: $f$ is smooth and constant in a neighborhood of $i^{-1}(\partial \ i(X))$
conclusions: $i_* f$ is also smooth

nodes.name: Time-one map F of a Hamiltonian
nodes.statement: Assume additionally that $X,Y$ are symplectic manifolds, $i$ is a symplectomorphism, and $f: S^1 \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ is a Hamiltonian function. Then $f$ induces the time-one-map of its flow; let it be denoted $F: X \to X$.

nodes.name: Pushforward of a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism
nodes.statement: The \textit{pushforward} of $F$ through $i$ is denoted $i_* F: Y \to Y$, and is the time-one-map of the flow induced by $i_* f$.

nodes.name: Polterovich-Shelukhin theorem: powers_k infinite in genus >= 4
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma_4$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\geq 4$, equipped with an area form $\sigma_4$, and $k \geq 2$ an integer. Then $powers_k(\Sigma_4,\sigma_4) = \infty$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Outline of the original proofs and dependencies of claims
assumptions: $\Sigma_4$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\geq 4$, equipped with an area form $\sigma_4$
conclusions: $powers_k(\Sigma_4,\sigma_4) = \infty$
also_stated_at: It has been shown in~\cite{PS14} that for surfaces of genus $\geq 4$ the complement $Ham \setminus Powers_k$ contains an arbitrarily large ball, with respect to the metric introduced by Hofer.
nodes.label: thm:orig2

nodes.name: Alvarez-Gavela et al.: F_2 in the asymptotic cone, genus >= 4
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma_4$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\geq 4$, equipped with an area form $\sigma_4$. Then for any non-principal ultrafilter $\mathcal{U}$ on $2^{\mathbb{N}}$, there exists a monomorphism $F_2 \hookrightarrow Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(\Sigma_4),d_H)$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Outline of the original proofs and dependencies of claims
assumptions: $\Sigma_4$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $\geq 4$, equipped with an area form $\sigma_4$
conclusions: there exists a monomorphism $F_2 \hookrightarrow Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(\Sigma_4),d_H)$
also_stated_at: It has been shown in~\cite{10} that for a surface $M$ of genus $\geq 4$ any such cone of $Ham(M,\omega)$ contains a free group with 2 generators.

In~\cite{10}, D. Alvarez-Gavela et al. show that given a symplectic surface $M$ of genus $\geq 4$, there exists a monomorphism $F_2 \to Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(M))$, where $F_2$ is the free group on two generators, and therefore $Cone_\mathcal{U}(Ham(M))$ has a subgroup isomorphic to $F_2$.
nodes.label: thm:orig3

nodes.name: Incompressible embedding
nodes.statement: The deductions marked $*$ are a consequence of the fact that $i$ is constructed to be \textit{incompressible}, i.e. it induces injections $\pi_1(C) \hookrightarrow \pi_1(\Sigma_4)$ and $\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) \hookrightarrow \pi_0(\mathscr{L}\Sigma_4)$.

nodes.statement: Given Proposition~\ref{prop:main2}, Theorem~\ref{thm:orig2} is proven in Section 5.1 of~\cite{PS14}, and given Proposition~\ref{prop:main}, Theorem~\ref{thm:4} is proven in Section 5.4 of~\cite{10} (the case where $w$ is not conjugate to a power of $V$ or $H$ requires Proposition~\ref{prop:main}; the case where $w$ is conjugate to a power of $V$ or $H$ does not use it).
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Outline of the original proofs and dependencies of claims
nodes.statement_short: Pointer to the cited works: Floer-theoretic deduction of the theorems from the fixed-point propositions.

nodes.name: Surface Sigma_4 of genus at least 4
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma_4$ be a surface of genus $\geq 4$.

nodes.name: Cylinder C_*
nodes.statement: Consider the cylinder $C_*=[-1,1]\times\mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z}$, for $L > 4$, with coordinates $x,y$ and the standard symplectic form $dx\wedge dy$.

nodes.name: Copies C_V, C_H
nodes.statement: Denote by $C_V,C_H$ two copies of $C_*$.

nodes.name: Squares S'_0, S'_1
nodes.statement: Consider the squares \[ S_0^\prime = [-1,1]\times[-1,1]/L\mathbb{Z}, S_1^\prime = [-1,1]\times[L/2-1,L/2+1]/L\mathbb{Z} \] in $C_*$.

nodes.name: Gluing symplectomorphism VH_{0,1}
nodes.statement: Define the symplectomorphism $VH_{0,1}:S_{V,0}\bigsqcup S_{V,1} \to S_{H,0} \bigsqcup S_{H,1}$ given by $VH\bigsqcup VH^\prime$, where \begin{myequation} VH:S_{V,0}\to S_{H,0} : (x,[y]) \mapsto (-y,[x]) ,\\ VH^\prime : S_{V,1}\to S_{H,1} : (x,[y]) \mapsto (y-L/2, [-x+L/2]) . \end{myequation}

nodes.name: Manifold C
nodes.statement: Define \[ C = C_V \bigcup_{VH_{0,1}} C_H . \]

nodes.name: Symplectic form omega_0 on C
nodes.statement: This is a symplectic manifold with symplectic form $\omega_0 = dx \wedge dy$ on every copy of the cylinder $C_*$.

nodes.name: Injections C_V, C_H into C
nodes.statement: Denote by $C_V: C_* \hookrightarrow C, \ C_H: C_* \hookrightarrow C$ the two injections induced by the above union.

nodes.name: Squares S_0, S_1 in C
nodes.statement: Denote by $S_0,S_1 \subset C$ the identification of the squares $S_{V,0},S_{H,0}$ and $S_{V,1},S_{H,1}$.

nodes.name: Base points s_0, s_1
nodes.statement: Fix two points $s_0 \in S_0, s_1 \in S_1$.

nodes.name: Paths q_1, ..., q_4
nodes.statement: Define 4 paths: two paths $q_1,q_3$ from $s_0$ to $s_1$, and two paths $q_2,q_4$ from $s_1$ to $s_0$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:qs}); $q_1, q_2$ are paths on $C_V$, and $q_3,q_4$ are paths on $C_H$.

nodes.name: pi_1(C) is free of rank 3
nodes.statement: Note that $\pi_1(C,s_0) \simeq F_3$, the free group on 3 generators.
conclusions: $\pi_1(C,s_0) \simeq F_3$

nodes.name: Generators a, b, c of pi_1(C, s_0)
nodes.statement: The 3 generators $a,b,c$ of $\pi_1(C,s_0)$ are taken to be: \begin{myequation} a = [q_1 \# q_2]_{\pi_1(C,s_0)} , \\ b = [q_3 \# q_4]_{\pi_1(C,s_0)} , \\ c = [q_3 \# q_2]_{\pi_1(C,s_0)} , \end{myequation} where the $\#$ sign is used for path concatenation: $q\#q^\prime$ is the concatenation of paths $q$ and then $q^\prime$, if $q(1) = q^\prime(0)$.

nodes.name: Profile function u_0
nodes.statement: Consider the function $u_0: [-1,1] \to \mathbb{R}$, $u_0(s) = 1 - |s|$.

nodes.name: Smoothing u of u_0
nodes.statement: Take an even, non-negative, sufficiently $C^0$-close smoothing $u$ to $u_0$ such that $u$ is supported away from $\{\pm 1\}$, and both $u-u_0$ and $\int_{-1}^t (u(s)-u_0(s)) ds$ are supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $\{\pm 1, 0\}$.

nodes.name: Shear map f_k on the cylinder
nodes.statement: For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, define \begin{myequation} f = f_k: C_* \to C_* , \\ f(x,[y]) = (x,[y + k L \cdot u(x)]) . \end{myequation}

nodes.name: Hamiltonian h_k of the shear map
nodes.statement: This mapping is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism on $C_*$ with Hamiltonian \[ h_k(x,[y]) = -\frac{k}{2} + k \int_{-1}^x u(s) ds . \]

nodes.name: Shear maps f_{k,V}, f_{k,H} on C
nodes.statement: Denote $f_{k,V} = (c_V)_* f_k$, $f_{k,H} = (c_H)_* f_k$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism Psi_k : F_2 -> Ham_c(C)
nodes.statement: Define a homomorphism \begin{myequation} \Psi_k: F_2 = \langle V,H \rangle \to Ham_c(C,\omega_0) ,\\ V \mapsto f_{k,V}, H \mapsto f_{k,H} , \end{myequation} where $Ham_c(M,\omega)$ denotes the group of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms whose generators have compact support of a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$.

nodes.name: Eggbeater maps
nodes.statement: Note that the image of a word $w = V^{N_1} H^{M_1} ... V^{N_r} H^{M_r} \in F_2$ is $f_{k,H}^{M_r} \circ f_{k,V}^{N_r} \circ ... \circ f_{k,H}^{M_1} \circ f_{k,V}^{N_1}$. These images are called \textit{eggbeater maps}.

nodes.name: Flow psi_{k,w}(t) on C
nodes.statement: Pushing forward the flow generated by $h_k$ to $C$, one gets flows on $C_V$ and $C_H$ whose time-one-maps are $f_{k,V}$ and $f_{k,H}$, and concatenating these in the order induced by $w$ (as in the construction of $\Psi_k(w)$) one gets a flow $\psi_{k,w}(t): C \to C$, whose time-one-map is $\Psi_k(w)$.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian G_{k,w}
nodes.statement: Denote the Hamiltonian that generates this flow $G_{k,w}: S^1 \times C \to \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Incompressible symplectic embedding i : C -> Sigma_4
nodes.statement: Consider a symplectic embedding $i: C \hookrightarrow \Sigma_4$ such that $i_*: \pi_1(C) \to \pi_1(\Sigma_4)$ and $\tau_i: \pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) \to \pi_0(\mathscr{L}\Sigma_4)$ are both injective, and such that each component of $\partial C$ separates $\Sigma_4$.

nodes.name: Homomorphisms Phi_k : F_2 -> Ham(Sigma_4)
nodes.statement: The homomorphisms $\Phi_k: F_2 \to Ham(\Sigma_4)$ will be defined by $\Phi_k(w) = i_* \Psi_k(w)$.

nodes.name: Phi_k(w) is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism
nodes.statement: The mapping $\Phi_k(w)$ is indeed a diffeomorphism, because of the assumptions on $u$, and is Hamiltonian, since it is generated by the Hamiltonian $H_{k,w} = i_* G_{k,w}$.
conclusions: The mapping $\Phi_k(w)$ is indeed a diffeomorphism
is Hamiltonian

nodes.name: Free homotopy classes alpha_{k,w} and beta_{k,w}
nodes.statement: Given $k \in \mathbb{N}, w = V^{N_1} H^{M_1} ... V^{N_r} H^{M_r} \in F_2$, set the free homotopy classes $\alpha_{k,w}$ to be \[ \alpha_{k,w} = \eta_{C,s_0}(\beta_{k,w}) \in \pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) , \] where \[ \beta_{k,w} = \Pi_{j=1}^r a^{k \cdot sign(N_j)} b^{k \cdot sign(M_j)} \in \pi_1(C,s_0) \] and $sign: \mathbb{Z} \to \{0, \pm1\}$ is \begin{myequation} n \mapsto \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{n}{|n|} & n \neq 0 \\ 0 & n = 0 \end{array}\right. . \end{myequation}
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha_{k,w}$ is the free class of $\beta_{k,w}=\prod a^{k\,sign(N_j)} b^{k\,sign(M_j)}$.

nodes.name: Parameters nu_j, mu_j
nodes.statement:
Additionally, choose $
u_j,\mu_j \in (0,1)$ for $j=1,...,r$ such that $ rac{
u_j}{L}, rac{\mu_j}{L} \in \mathbb{Q}$ for all $j$, and the values $\sum_{j=0}^{r-1} (\epsilon_{2j+1}(1-\mu_{j+1})^2 - \epsilon_{2j+4}(1-
u_{j+1})^2)$ are all distinct, for all sign vectors $\vec\epsilon = (\epsilon_0,...,\epsilon_{2r-1}) \in \{\pm 1\}^{2r}$.

nodes.name: Index set K
nodes.statement: For these choices, the set $K \subset \mathbb{N}$ from Proposition~\ref{prop:main2} is taken to be $K = \{k \in \mathbb{N} | \forall j: \frac{\mu_j k}{L}, \frac{\nu_j k}{L} \in \mathbb{Z} \}$.

nodes.name: Free homotopy classes alpha'_k and beta'_k
nodes.statement: For $k \in K$ set \[ \alpha_k^\prime = \eta_{C,s_0}(\beta_k^\prime) \in \pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) , \] where \[ \beta_k^\prime = \Pi_{j=1}^r a^{\frac{\nu_j k}{L}} b^{\frac{\mu_j k}{L}} \in \pi_1(C,s_0) . \]

nodes.name: Reduction of Propositions 3.7, 3.8 to claims on C
nodes.statement: The outline of the proofs of Propositions~\ref{prop:main},~\ref{prop:main2} is as follows. Since any non-degenerate fixed point of $\Phi_k(w)$ must lie in $\mathrm{Im} i$, and in addition $i: C \to \Sigma_4$, $i_*: \pi_1(C,s_0) \to \pi_1(\Sigma_4,i(s_0))$ and $\tau_i: \pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) \to \pi_0(\mathscr{L}\Sigma_4)$ are all injective, it is enough to prove versions of Propositions~\ref{prop:main},~\ref{prop:main2} on $C$, i.e. prove the following claims:
nodes.statement_short: Since $i$ is incompressible and fixed points lie in its image, it suffices to prove the analogous statements on $C$.

nodes.name: Fixed points of Psi_k(w) in class alpha_{k,w} on C
nodes.statement: Let $w = \Pi_{j=1}^r V^{N_j} H^{M_j} \in F_2$ be balanced. For large enough $k \in \mathbb{N}$, there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $\Psi_k(w)$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\alpha_{k,w}$, and these fixed points have actions (with respect to $G_{k,w}$) and Conley-Zehnder indices as in Equations~\ref{eq:2},\ref{eq:3}.
conclusions: there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $\Psi_k(w)$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\alpha_{k,w}$, and these fixed points have actions (with respect to $G_{k,w}$) and Conley-Zehnder indices as in Equations~\ref{eq:2},\ref{eq:3}
nodes.label: cl:2

nodes.name: Fixed points of Psi_k(w) in class alpha'_k with action gaps on C
nodes.statement: Let $w = (VH)^r \in F_2$ for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$. For large enough $k \in K$, there are $2^{2r}$ fixed points of $\Psi_k(w)$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\alpha_k^\prime$, and such fixed points in different orbits have action gaps (with respect to $G_{k,w}$) that grow linearly with $k$ as $k \to \infty$.
conclusions: there are $2^{2r}$ fixed points of $\Psi_k(w)$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\alpha_k^\prime$, and such fixed points in different orbits have action gaps (with respect to $G_{k,w}$) that grow linearly with $k$ as $k \to \infty$
nodes.label: cl:2.2

nodes.name: Sketch of proof of Claims 3.9, 3.10 (cited)
nodes.statement: This is proven in two steps. First, one proves these claims with respect to a piecewise-linear version $\psi_{k,w}^\prime(t)$ of the isotopy $\psi_{k,w}(t)$. This is done in Subsection 5.1 of~\cite{10} and in Section 5 of~\cite{PS14}, by analysis of the dynamics on $C$. Then, one shows that the non-degenerate fixed points of $\Psi_k(w)$ are exactly those of $\psi_{k,w}^\prime(1)$, for $k$ large enough. This is done in Subsection 5.3 of~\cite{10}.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the claims for a piecewise-linear isotopy, then show its non-degenerate fixed points coincide with those of $\Psi_k(w)$ for large $k$.

nodes.name: Data D, e_2, i_2, Xi_k for genus 2, 3
nodes.statement: The following data will be defined: \begin{itemize} \item A symplectic surface $(D,\omega)$ that contains $C$ from the original construction (i.e. $e_2: C \hookrightarrow D$ is a symplectic embedding that induces an embedding $\tau_{e_2}: \pi_0(\mathscr{L}C) \hookrightarrow \pi_0(\mathscr{L}D)$), \item an injection $i_2: D \hookrightarrow \Sigma$, and \item homomorphisms $\Xi_k: F_2 \to Ham_c(D, \omega)$ indexed by $k \in \mathbb{N}$, with $\Xi_k(w)$ the time-one-map of the flow $\xi_{k,w}(t): D \to D$, such that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}, w \in F_2$: $\xi_{k,w}(t) \restriction_C = \psi_{k,w}(t)$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A surface $D\supset C$, an embedding $i_2: D\to\Sigma$, and homomorphisms $\Xi_k$ whose flows restrict to $\psi_{k,w}$ on $C$.

nodes.name: Pushforward dynamics on Sigma via i_2
nodes.statement: In order to work on $\Sigma$, the dynamics will be pushed forward by $i_2$. This will result in a Hamiltonian $(i_2)_* F_{k,w}: S^1 \times \Sigma \to \mathbb{R}$, and the flow and time-one-map it generates, denoted $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}(t): \Sigma \to \Sigma$ and $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w): \Sigma \to \Sigma$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 from Propositions 3.11, 3.12
nodes.statement: With these constructions in hand, we will prove new versions of Propositions~\ref{prop:main},~\ref{prop:main2}, and these will imply the generalized Theorems~\ref{thm:2},~\ref{thm:3}. These dependencies are depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:new_depends}. The deductions marked $**$ can be taken as is from the proofs for surfaces of genus $\geq 4$ in~\cite{PS14},~\cite{10}. The deductions marked $*$ will now require justification, since $i_2$ will no longer be incompressible. Since Claims~\ref{cl:2},~\ref{cl:2.2} were already established (see proof in~\cite{PS14},~\cite{10} or sketch in Subsection~\ref{sec:3.1}), we have to show why they imply Propositions~\ref{prop:new},~\ref{prop:new2}. This is done in Subsection~\ref{sec:3.2.2}, and uses Lemma~\ref{lemma:2}.
nodes.statement_short: New versions of Propositions 3.7, 3.8 imply the theorems via the cited Floer-theoretic deductions; only the incompressibility step needs Lemma 1.3.

nodes.name: Fixed points of (i_2)_* Xi_k(w) in class tau_{i_2}(alpha_{k,w})
nodes.statement: Let $w = \Pi_{j=1}^r V^{N_j} H^{M_j} \in F_2 = \langle H,V \rangle$ be balanced. For large enough $k \in \mathbb{N}$, there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ in $\Sigma$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$, and such fixed points have actions and Conley-Zehnder indices as in Equations~\ref{eq:2},\ref{eq:3}.
assumptions: $w = \Pi_{j=1}^r V^{N_j} H^{M_j} \in F_2 = \langle H,V \rangle$ be balanced
conclusions: there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ in $\Sigma$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$, and such fixed points have actions and Conley-Zehnder indices as in Equations~\ref{eq:2},\ref{eq:3}
nodes.statement_short: Genus 2,3 version of Proposition 3.7 for the eggbeater maps pushed forward by $i_2$.
nodes.label: prop:new

nodes.name: Fixed points of (i_2)_* Xi_k(w) in class tau_{i_2}(alpha'_k) with action gaps
nodes.statement: Let $w = (VH)^r \in F_2$ for some $r \in \mathbb{N}$. For large enough $k \in K$, there are $2^{2r}$ fixed points of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ in $\Sigma$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$, and such fixed points in different orbits have action gaps that grow linearly with $k$: for such fixed points in different orbits $y, z$: \[ | \mathcal{A}(y) - \mathcal{A}(z) | \geq c \cdot k + O(1) , \] as $k \to \infty$, for some global constant $c > 0$. The set $K \subset \mathbb{N}$ is as defined in Subsection~\ref{sec:3.1}.
conclusions: there are $2^{2r}$ fixed points of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ in $\Sigma$ whose orbits have free homotopy class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$, and such fixed points in different orbits have action gaps that grow linearly with $k$

nodes.name: Additional cylinders C_1, C_2
nodes.statement: Consider $C$, defined in Subsection~\ref{sec:geometric}, and two additional copies of the cylinder $C_*$, $C_1$ and $C_2$.

nodes.name: Surface D
nodes.statement: Our manifold $D$ will be $D = C \bigsqcup C_1 \bigsqcup C_2$, equipped with the standard symplectic form $\omega_0 = dx \wedge dy$ on every component.

nodes.name: Inclusions c_1, c_2
nodes.statement: Denote the symplectic inclusions $C_* \hookrightarrow C_1,C_2$ by $c_1,c_2$ respectively.

nodes.name: Embedding i_2 on C and handle placement
nodes.statement: The symplectic embedding $i_2:(D,\omega_0) \hookrightarrow (\Sigma, \sigma)$ is built in stages. First define $i_2$ on $C$: embed $C$ symplectically into $\mathbb{R}^2$, embed the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ into $S^2$, and then add 2 handles as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:handles}; that is, $C$ seperates the sphere into 4 connected components, each having two neighbors; connect any two non-neighboring components with a handle. In the case of genus 3, add a handle inside the 'outside' component to obtain a surface of genus 3 (we will refer to this handle as the extra handle). This defines $i_2 \restriction_C$. Define $i_2$ on $C_1 \bigsqcup C_2$ by embedding each of them symplectically into one of the non-extra handles (with $C_1$ and $C_2$ on different handles), such that the images $i_2(C_1), i_2(C_2)$ are not contractible. The orientation of the embeddings $i_2\restriction_{C_1}, i_2\restriction_{C_2}$, and which goes on which handle, will be defined immediately. The embedding $i_2$ can be seen in Figure~\ref{fig:handles}.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $C$ in $S^2$, join non-neighbouring complementary components by 2 handles (plus an extra one for genus 3), and put $C_1,C_2$ on the handles.

nodes.name: Base points s'_k
nodes.statement: Fix some $s^\prime_k \in C_k$ for $k=1,2$.

nodes.name: Generators d_k of pi_1(C_k)
nodes.statement: The generators of $\pi_1(C_k,s^\prime_k) = \mathbb{Z}$ are denoted $d_k$. These are positively oriented - that is, $d_k = [t\mapsto(0,Lt) \in C_k]$ as elements in $\pi_1(C_k,s_k^\prime)$.

nodes.name: Generators g_1, ..., g_4 of pi_1(Sigma)
nodes.statement: Denote the generators of $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$ by $g_1,..,g_4$, such that $\pi_1 (\Sigma, i_2(s_0)) = \left\langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4\middle|[g_1,g_2] [g_3,g_4] \right\rangle$, and the loops $g_1$ and $g_3$ go around the two handles (see Figure~\ref{fig:gens}).

nodes.name: Generators g_1, ..., g_6 in genus 3
nodes.statement: In the case where $\Sigma$ is of genus 3, denote $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0)) = \langle g_1, ..., g_6 | [g_1,g_2] [g_3,g_4] [g_5,g_6] \rangle$, such that the loops $g_1$ and $g_3$ still go around the two non-extra handles (the same as in Figure~\ref{fig:gens}), and such that $g_5$ goes around the extra handle. The loops $g_{k+1}$ go along the handle that the loops $g_k$ go around (for $k = 1,3,5$), oriented such that $[g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4][g_5,g_6] = 1$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$.
nodes.statement_short: In genus 3, $g_5$ goes around the extra handle and $g_{k+1}$ along the handle that $g_k$ circles.

nodes.name: Placement and orientation of i_2 on C_1, C_2
nodes.statement: Choose the image of $C_1$ to be contained in the handle that the loop $g_1 \in \pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$ goes around (in Figures~\ref{fig:handles} and~\ref{fig:gens} this is the upper handle), and so $i_2(C_2)$ is contained in the handle that the loop $g_3$ goes around. Since the image of $C_1$ is located on a handle, is non-contractible, and $i_2$ is an embedding, one can choose how to orient the image of $C_1$: \[ \tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_1,s_1^\prime} (d_1) = \eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_1) \text{ or } \tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_1,s_1^\prime} (d_1) = \eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_1^{-1}) , \] and similiarly one can choose the orientation of $i_2(C_2)$: \[ \tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_2,s_2^\prime} (d_2) = \eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_3) \text{ or } \tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_2,s_2^\prime} (d_2) = \eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_3^{-1}) . \] Choose the orientation of the embeddings $i_2\restriction_{C_1}, i_2\restriction_{C_2}$ to be such that the elements $d_1,d_2$ map to $\eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_1)$ and $\eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)} (g_3^{-1})$, respectively, under $\tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_k, s_k^\prime}$ (for $k = 1,2$). This concludes the definition of the embedding $i_2$.
nodes.statement_short: $C_1$ goes on the $g_1$ handle and $C_2$ on the $g_3$ handle, oriented so that $d_1\mapsto g_1$ and $d_2\mapsto g_3^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Action of (i_2)_* on generators a, b, c
nodes.statement: By construction of $i_2: D \hookrightarrow \Sigma$, the pushforward $(i_2)_*: \pi_1(D, s_0) \to \pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$ acts on the generators $a,b,c$ of $\pi_1(D,s_0)$ so: \begin{myequation} a \mapsto g_1 g_3 , \\ b \mapsto g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3 , \\ c \mapsto g_3 . \end{myequation}
conclusions: a \mapsto g_1 g_3 , \\ b \mapsto g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3 , \\ c \mapsto g_3 .

nodes.name: Autonomous Hamiltonians g_{k,V}, g_{k,H} on D
nodes.statement: Define two autonomous Hamiltonians on $D$: \begin{myequation} g_{k,V}: D \to \mathbb{R} , \\ g_{k,V} = (e_2 \circ c_V)_* h_k \bigsqcup - (c_1)_* h_k \bigsqcup (c_2)_* h_k ; \\ g_{k,H}: D \to \mathbb{R} , \\ g_{k,H} = (e_2 \circ c_H)_* h_k \bigsqcup (c_1)_* h_k \bigsqcup (c_2)_* h_k . \\ \end{myequation}

nodes.name: Flow xi_{k,w}(t) on D
nodes.statement: Given $w \in F_2 = \langle V,H \rangle$, define $\xi_{k,w}(t)$, the flow on $D$, as the concatenation of the flows induced by $g_{k,V}, g_{k,H}$, in the order induced by $w$.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian F_{k,w} and time-one map Xi_k(w)
nodes.statement: The Hamiltonian which induces this flow is denoted $F_{k,w}: S^1 \times D \to \mathbb{R}$, and its time-one-map is $\Xi_k(w): D \to D$.
also_stated_at: The Hamiltonian generating $\xi_{k,w}(t)$ will be denoted $F_{k,w}: S^1 \times D \to \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: F_{k,w} and i_2 satisfy the pushforward condition
nodes.statement: Next, note that $F_{k,w}$ and $i_2$ satisfy Condition~\ref{eq:condition} for all $k,w$.
conclusions: $F_{k,w}$ and $i_2$ satisfy Condition~\ref{eq:condition} for all $k,w$

nodes.name: Free homotopy classes of eggbeater orbits
nodes.statement: Let $\tilde{\gamma} : S^1 \to C$ be a closed $\psi_{k,w}$-orbit. Then there exist $k_1,...,k_r, l_1,...,l_r \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u_1,...,u_r, v_1,...,v_r \in \{0,1\}$ such that $[\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \eta_{C,s_0}(\Pi_{m=1}^r a^{k_m}c^{-u_m}b^{l_m}c^{v_m})$.
conclusions: there exist $k_1,...,k_r, l_1,...,l_r \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u_1,...,u_r, v_1,...,v_r \in \{0,1\}$ such that $[\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \eta_{C,s_0}(\Pi_{m=1}^r a^{k_m}c^{-u_m}b^{l_m}c^{v_m})$
nodes.statement_short: Every closed eggbeater orbit in $C$ has free class of the form $\prod a^{k_m}c^{-u_m}b^{l_m}c^{v_m}$.
nodes.label: claim:3

nodes.name: Partial injectivity of tau_{i_2}
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma = \eta_{D,s_0}(\Pi_{m=1}^r a^{k_m}c^{-u_m}b^{l_m}c^{v_m}) \in \pi_0(\mathscr{L}D)$ for some $k_1,...,k_r,l_1,...,l_r \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u_1,...,u_r,v_1,...,v_r \in \{0,1\}$, and assume $\tau_{i_2}(\gamma) = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$. Then $\gamma = \alpha_{k,w}$. Alternatively, if $k \in K$, assume $\tau_{i_2}(\gamma) = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$. Then $\gamma = \alpha_k^\prime$.
conclusions: $\gamma = \alpha_{k,w}$
$\gamma = \alpha_k^\prime$
$\gamma = \alpha_{k,w}$
$\gamma = \alpha_k^\prime$

nodes.statement_short: Among classes of the orbit form, $\tau_{i_2}$ does not merge anything with $\alpha_{k,w}$ or $\alpha'_k$.
nodes.label: claim:4

nodes.name: Relevant fixed points lie in i_2(C)
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ be large enough, and let $z \in \Sigma$ be a non-degenerate fixed point of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ whose $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}$-orbit is in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$, i.e. $[(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}(t) (z)]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}\Sigma)} = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$. Alternatively, let $k \in K$ be large enough, and let $z \in \Sigma$ be a non-degenerate fixed point of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ whose $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}$-orbit is in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$. In both cases, $z \in i_2(C)$. \\
assumptions: $z \in \Sigma$ be a non-degenerate fixed point of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ whose $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}$-orbit is in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$
conclusions: $z \in i_2(C)$
nodes.statement_short: Non-degenerate fixed points in the classes $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$ or $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha'_k)$ lie in the image of $C$, not on the extra annuli.
nodes.label: claim:5

nodes.name: Proof of Propositions 3.11, 3.12
nodes.statement: Recall that Claims~\ref{cl:2},~\ref{cl:2.2}, proven in~\cite{10},~\cite{PS14}, are analogous to these propositions, but set in $C$. We want to show why they imply that these propositions hold in $\Sigma$. The proofs for both propositions are very similar, so we present them simultaneously. Let $\tilde{\gamma}: S^1 \to \Sigma$ be a closed orbit of $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}(t)$ in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$ (or $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$, in the case where $k \in K$) such that $z = \tilde{\gamma}(0)$ is a non-degenerate fixed point of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$. By Claim~\ref{claim:5}, if $k$ is large enough then $z \in i_2(C)$, therefore $y = i_2^{-1}(z) \in C$ is uniquely defined. Denote by $\tilde{\gamma_y} : S^1 \to C$ the $\xi_{k,w}(t)$-orbit of $y$. By Claim~\ref{claim:3}, there exist $k_1,...,k_r, l_1,...,l_r \in \mathbb{Z} , u_1,...,u_r, v_1,...,v_r \in \{0,1\}$ such that \[ [\tilde{\gamma_y}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \eta_{C,s_0}(\Pi_{m=1}^r a^{k_m}c^{-u_m}b^{l_m}c^{v_m}) . \] Since $\tau_{i_2}([\tilde{\gamma_y}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)}) = [\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}\Sigma)} = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$ (or $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$), one has $[\tilde{\gamma_y}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \alpha_{k,w}$ (or $[\tilde{\gamma_y}]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \alpha_k^\prime$) by Claim~\ref{claim:4}. Thus non-degenerate fixed points of $(i_2)_* \Xi_k(w)$ in $\Sigma$ whose orbits are in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$ correspond in a 1-1 manner to non-degenerate fixed points of $\Xi_k(w)$ in $D$ whose orbits are in the class $\alpha_{k,w}$ (and there is a similar correspondence for the classes $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime),\alpha_k^\prime$). Note that since Claim~\ref{claim:4} uses Lemma~\ref{lemma:2}, this is the point where the algebraic Lemma~\ref{lemma:2} enters the proof. \\ Therefore it is enough to restrict the analysis to the dynamics on $D$, and further, to the dynamics on $C$, since $z \in i_2(C)$. By Claim~\ref{cl:2}, for large enough $k$ there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $\Xi_k(w)$ in the class $\alpha_{k,w}$, indexed by $\vec{\epsilon} = (\epsilon_0,...,\epsilon_{2r-1}) \in \{\pm 1\}^{2r}$, such that their actions and Conley-Zehnder indices are given by Equations~\ref{eq:2},\ref{eq:3}. Since $i_2$ preserves actions and Conley-Zehnder indices by construction, this proves Proposition~\ref{prop:new}. Similarly, setting $w = (VH)^r$, by Claim~\ref{cl:2.2} for large enough $k \in K$ there are $2^{2r}$ non-degenerate fixed points of $\Xi_k(w)$ in the class $\alpha_k^\prime$, such that fixed points in different orbits have action gaps that grow linearly with $k$. The injection $i_2$ preserves actions, so this proves Proposition~\ref{prop:new2}.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points lie in $i_2(C)$ (Claim 3.15), their classes have the orbit form (Claim 3.13), so partial injectivity (Claim 3.14) reduces to Claims 3.9, 3.10 on $C$.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 3.13
nodes.statement: Denote $z = \tilde{\gamma}(0)$. Recall that $\psi_{k,w}^\prime$ is the piecewise-linear version of $\psi_{k,w}$ defined in Subsection~\ref{sec:3.1}, and that it is the concatenation of some autonomous Hamiltonian isotopies $f_{0,V}^{N_1t}, f_{0,H}^{M_1t}, ...$; while $\psi_{k,w}$ is their composition. Thus $\tilde{\gamma}$ and $t \mapsto \psi_{k,w}^\prime(t) (z)$ are freely homotopic loops in $C$. Therefore, it is enough to show there exist some $k_1,...,k_r, l_1,...,l_r \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u_1,...,u_r, v_1,...,v_r \in \{0,1\}$ such that $[t \mapsto \psi_{k,w}^\prime(t) (z)]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C)} = \eta_{C,s_0}(\Pi_{m=1}^r a^{k_m} c^{-u_m} b^{l_m} c^{v_m})$, since homotopic loops have the same $\eta_{C,s_0}$-images. This is shown in the proof of Lemma 4.2 in~\cite{10} - in their notation, $\psi_{k,w}^\prime(t)$ is denoted $\phi^t$, and $k_\mu, l_\mu, u_\mu, v_\mu$ are denoted $n_\mu, m_\mu, \epsilon_\mu, \nu_\mu$ respectively, for $1 \leq \mu \leq r$ (note we do not need the whole statement of Lemma 4.2).
nodes.statement_short: The orbit is freely homotopic to that of the piecewise-linear isotopy, whose class was computed in Lemma 4.2 of [10].

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 3.14
nodes.statement: The two assumptions are similar, and the proofs for the two cases are the same. For concreteness, assume $\tau_{i_2}(\gamma) = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$, the other case is analogous. Let $\delta \in \pi_1(C,s_0)$ be any element such that $\gamma = \eta_{C,s_0}(\delta)$. By assumption, $\tau_{i_2}(\gamma) = \tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$. Commutativity implies $\eta_{\Sigma,i_2(s_0)}((i_2)_* \delta) = \eta_{\Sigma,i_2(s_0)}((i_2)_* \beta_{k,w})$, so one sees that $(i_2)_* \delta$ and $(i_2)_* \beta_{k,w}$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$. In the case where the genus of $\Sigma$ is 2, recall that $\pi_1(D,s_0) = F_3$, and that $(i_2)_* : F_3 \to \pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$ is exactly the same homomorphism as in the requirements of Lemma~\ref{lemma:2}. In the case where the genus of $\Sigma$ is 3, denote \begin{myequation} p_{1234}: \pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0)) \to \langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4] \rangle , \\ g_1 \mapsto g_1, g_2 \mapsto g_2, g_3 \mapsto g_3, g_4 \mapsto g_4 , \\ g_5,g_6 \mapsto 1 , \end{myequation} and note that $p_{1234} \circ (i_2)_*$ is exactly the homomorphism as in the requirements of Lemma~\ref{lemma:2}. Since $(i_2)_* \delta, (i_2)_* \beta_{k,w}$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$, so are $(p_{1234} \circ (i_2)_*) (\delta), (p_{1234} \circ (i_2)_*) (\beta_{k,w})$ in $\langle g_1,g_2,g_3,g_4 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4] \rangle$. In both cases, one can get by Lemma~\ref{lemma:2} that $\delta$ and $\beta_{k,w}$ are conjugate in $\pi_1(D,s_0)$, so $\gamma = \eta_{D,s_0}(\delta) = \eta_{D,s_0}(\beta_{k,w}) = \alpha_{k,w}$ by definition of $\eta_{D,s_0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Commutativity turns equal free classes into conjugate images; in genus 2 directly, in genus 3 after projecting by $p_{1234}$, Lemma 1.3 gives conjugacy in $F_3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 3.15
nodes.statement: Under both of the assumptions (that the orbit of $z$ is in the class $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_{k,w})$ or $\tau_{i_2}(\alpha_k^\prime)$), the orbit of $z$ is in the class $\eta_{\Sigma, i_2(s_0)}(\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3)^{k_{2m}})$ for some sequence $k_1,...,k_{2r} \in \mathbb{Z}$, since $(i_2)_*(a) = g_1 g_3, (i_2)_*(b) = g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1} g_3$. Note that for large enough $k$, the elements $k_m$ in this sequence all satisfy $|k_m| \geq 2$. As noted in Section~\ref{sec:2}, $\pi_1(\Sigma)$ is a free product of $H_1 = \langle g_1,g_2 \rangle, H_2 = \langle g_3,g_4 \rangle$ with amalgamation of subgroups $A = \langle [g_1,g_2] \rangle, B = \langle [g_3,g_4] \rangle$ by the isomorphism $\phi: A \to B: [g_1,g_2] \mapsto [g_3,g_4]^{-1}$. In the case where the genus of $\Sigma$ is 3, $\pi_1(\Sigma)$ is a free product of $H_1 = \langle g_1,g_2 \rangle, H_2 = \langle g_3,g_4,g_5,g_6 \rangle$ with amalgamation of subgroups $A = \langle [g_1,g_2] \rangle, B = \langle [g_3,g_4][g_5,g_6] \rangle$ by the isomorphism $\phi : A \to B : [g_1,g_2] \mapsto ([g_3,g_4][g_5,g_6])^{-1}$. Note that $z \in i_2(D)$, else $z$ is a degenerate fixed point. Assume by contradiction $z \in i_2(C_1 \cup C_2)$. Denote the orbit of $z$ under $(i_2)_* \xi_{k,w}(t)$ by $\tilde{\gamma}: S^1 \to \Sigma$. If $z \in i_2(C_1)$, then $\tilde{\gamma}(t) \in i_2(C_1)$ for all $t$, since $\tilde{\gamma}(t) \in i_2(D)$ for all $t$, and $C_1$ is a connected component of $D$. This means $\tilde{\gamma}$ is (freely) homotopic to some loop $\tilde{\delta}: S^1 \to \Sigma$ based in $i_2(s_0)$ with $[\tilde{\delta}]_{\pi_1(\Sigma,i_2(s_0))} = g_1^n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, since by construction $\tau_{i_2} \circ \eta_{C_1, s_1^\prime} (d_1) = \eta_{\Sigma,i_2(s_0)} (g_1)$ (recall that $d_1$ is the homotopy class of a loop going around $i_2(C_1)$ once). Denote the homotopy between $\tilde{\gamma},\tilde{\delta}$ by $F : S^1 \times [0,1] \to \Sigma$ with $F(\cdot,0) = \tilde{\gamma}, F(\cdot, 1) = \tilde{\delta}$. Then $\rho = F(0, \cdot)$ is a loop in $\Sigma$ based in $i_2(s_0)$, and $[\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_1(\Sigma,i_2(s_0))} = [\rho \# \tilde{\delta} \# \overline{\rho}]_{\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))}$. The following holds: \begin{myequation} \Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}} \sim \\ \sim [\tilde{\gamma}]_{\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))} = [\rho \# \tilde{\delta} \# \overline{\rho}]_{\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))} = \chi g_1^n \chi^{-1} , \end{myequation} where $\chi = [\rho]_{\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))}$. Thus $\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}} \sim g_1^n$. Note that $(g_1^n)$, a sequence with a single element, is a cyclically reduced sequence of $\langle H_1*H_2 , A=B, \phi \rangle$, so $g_1^n$ is a cyclically reduced element, with $len(g_1^n) = 1$. Recall that $w$ is given in cyclically reduced form, thus $\forall \ 1 \leq m \leq r: M_m, N_m \neq 0$. Since for all $m$, $|k_m| \geq 2$, by Claim~\ref{cl:length} it can be seen that $len \left(\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}} \right) > 1$, in contradiction. If the genus of $\Sigma$ is 3, then note that $p_{1234}$ (defined in the proof of Claim~\ref{claim:4}) preserves factors (in the sense of the proof of Claim~\ref{cl:length}), which means that $len(\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}}) = len(p_{1234}(\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}})) > 1$, by Claim~\ref{cl:length}. This is again a contradiction. Therefore $z \not\in i_2(C_1)$. Likewise, assume $z \in i_2(C_2)$. Similarly to the previous case, there is a conjugacy between $\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}}$ and $g_3^n$ in $\pi_1(\Sigma, i_2(s_0))$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. As before, $len(\Pi_{m=1}^r (g_1 g_3)^{k_{2m-1}} (g_2 g_1^{-1} g_2^{-1}g_3)^{k_{2m}}) > 1$ and $len(g_3^n) = 1$, but $len$ is conjugation-invariant, so this is a contradiction. All cases lead to a contradiction, therefore $z \in i_2(C)$.
nodes.statement_short: A fixed point on $C_1$ or $C_2$ would make the orbit class conjugate to a power of $g_1$ or $g_3$, of length 1, contradicting Claim 2.3 (length $>1$).

nodes.name: Alternative proof of Theorems 1.1, 1.2 in genus 3 via incompressibility
nodes.statement: This incompressibility will imply Theorems~\ref{thm:2},~\ref{thm:3} by following the original proofs in~\cite{PS14} and~\cite{10}.
nodes.statement_short: With an incompressible embedding of $C$ into genus 3, the original genus $\ge 4$ proofs apply verbatim.

nodes.name: Cylinder C_3 and surface E
nodes.statement: Let $C_3$ be another copy of $C_*$, and define $E = D \bigsqcup C_3$, with the symplectic form $dx \wedge dy$ on every component.

nodes.name: Inclusions c_3, e_3
nodes.statement: Denote by $c_3: C_* \to E, e_3: D \to E$ the symplectic inclusions.

nodes.name: Embedding i_3 : E -> Sigma_3
nodes.statement: The embedding $i_3: E \hookrightarrow \Sigma_3$ is defined in two parts. First, embed $C$ symplectically into $S^2$. Note that $C$ separates the sphere into 4 connected components. Choose any one of these components, and connect it with handles to the other 3 components, with one handle each. The result is a genus 3 surface $\Sigma_3$, and this defines $i_3 \restriction_C$. Define $i_3$ on $C_1 \bigsqcup C_2 \bigsqcup C_3$ by symplectically embedding each of them on a different handle. The embedding $i_3$ can be seen in Figure~\ref{fig:handles_gen_3}, and the generators of $\pi_1(\Sigma_3,i_3(s_0)) = \langle g_1,...,g_6 | [g_1,g_2][g_3,g_4][g_5,g_6] \rangle$ can be seen in Figure~\ref{fig:gens_gen_3}. The orientations of $i_3 \restriction_{C_j}$ for $j=1,2,3$ are chosen such that \begin{myequation} \tau_{e_3 \circ c_1} [t \mapsto (0,Lt)]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C_*)} = \eta_{\Sigma_3,i_3(s_0)}(g_1) ,\\ \tau_{e_3 \circ c_2} [t \mapsto (0,Lt)]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C_*)} = \eta_{\Sigma_3,i_3(s_0)}(g_3) ,\\ \tau_{c_3} [t \mapsto (0,Lt)]_{\pi_0(\mathscr{L}C_*)} = \eta_{\Sigma_3,i_3(s_0)}(g_5) . \end{myequation}

nodes.statement_short: Embed $C$ in $S^2$, join one complementary component to the other three by handles (genus 3), put $C_1,C_2,C_3$ on the handles with fixed orientations.

nodes.name: Action of (i_3)_* on generators a, b, c
nodes.statement: As can be seen in Figure~\ref{fig:gens_gen_3}, the induced homomorphism $(i_3)_*: F_3 \to \pi_1(\Sigma_3,i_3(s_0))$ acts on the generators $a,b,c$ of $F_3$ so: \begin{myequation} a \mapsto g_1 g_3 ,\\ b \mapsto g_3 g_5 ,\\ c \mapsto g_3 , \end{myequation} where $a,b,c \in \pi_1(C,s_0)$ are as defined in Subsection~\ref{sec:3.1}.
nodes.section: 4.1 The egg-beater surface and map, and the embedding
conclusions: a \mapsto g_1 g_3 ,\\ b \mapsto g_3 g_5 ,\\ c \mapsto g_3 ,

nodes.statement: The map $i_3 \restriction_C$ is incompressible, i.e. $(i_3 \restriction_C)_*$ and $\tau_{i_3 \restriction_C}$ are injective.

nodes.name: Eggbeater maps Theta_k on E
nodes.statement: Define the egg-beater maps on $E$ as follows: \begin{myequation} \Theta_k: F_2 \to Ham_c(E) ,\\ V \mapsto (e_3 \circ e_2 \circ c_V)_* f_k \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_1)_* f_k \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_2)_* f_k \bigsqcup 0 \restriction_{C_3} ,\\ H \mapsto (e_3 \circ e_2 \circ c_H)_* f_k \bigsqcup 0 \restriction_{C_1} \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_2)_* f_k \bigsqcup -(c_3)_* f_k . \end{myequation}
nodes.section: 4.1 The egg-beater surface and map, and the embedding

nodes.name: Theta_k are Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms
nodes.statement: These are Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms: $\Theta_k(V)$ can be seen to be generated by the Hamiltonian \[ (e_3 \circ e_2 \circ c_V)_* h_k \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_1)_* h_k \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_2)_* f_h \bigsqcup 0 \restriction_{C_3} , \] and $\Theta_k(H)$ by the Hamiltonian \[ (e_3 \circ e_2 \circ c_H)_* f_k \bigsqcup 0 \restriction_{C_1} \bigsqcup -(e_3 \circ c_2)_* f_k \bigsqcup -(c_3)_* f_k . \]
nodes.section: 4.1 The egg-beater surface and map, and the embedding
conclusions: These are Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms

nodes.name: Eggbeater maps on Sigma_3
nodes.statement: The egg-beater maps on $\Sigma_3$ are $(i_3)_* \Theta_k(w)$, for $w \in F_2$.
